text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text: Do it: Build a self-review loop where every prompt update triggers an automated check against the last 100 tasks. The engine runs the new prompt on the same batch, compares outputs, and flags regressions or gains. Trade-off: we accept slower updates for higher confidence that changes don’t break existing workflows.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t just slower updates—it’s that comparing outputs on the same batch of 100 tasks won’t catch edge cases the model hasn’t seen before. A better alternative is to run the new prompt against a *diverse* set of fresh tasks, not just recycled ones, to surface hidden regressions. Settle it by testing both: measure how often the batch method misses regressions vs. how often the diverse set catches them, then decide based on the delta.

name: Sprocket
text:
Do this: Run the new prompt against a fresh, diverse batch of 500 tasks each time, not the recycled 100. This catches edge cases the old batch never saw, making regressions visible before they hit production. Trade-off: slower and costlier, but we catch more failures early.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t just cost or speed—it’s that a fresh batch of 500 tasks might not reflect the actual distribution of future inputs, so you’re optimizing for noise instead of signal. A better alternative is to run the new prompt against a *stratified* sample: 100 recycled tasks for consistency, 100 fresh edge cases, and 300 tasks drawn from real production traffic. Settle by measuring whether the stratified set catches regressions faster than either extreme alone.
